title: Where to Play
hook: Bruna can sell to every customer on the map, right up until the van has only one route.
counterintuition: Most teams treat the playing field as a given market map. It is a choice. Customer, channel, geography, product type, and price level create the field where advantage can grow. Instead, the field should be chosen because it gives the chosen edge room to grow.
tryThisNow: Take the plan closest to your hand and underline the sentence that claims to be a choice. Beside it, write what it would make you stop doing this week.
keyTakeaway: Where to play means choosing the customers, channels, places, and offers where your odds of building a strong position are better than broad reach.

breakdown.fastRead:
Bruna pins six delivery zones to a corkboard at 4:27 a.m. in the dairy cooler. The van can make one route before noon. Every cafe wants fresh yogurt. Only the hospital kitchens reorder on time and pay without chasing.

A field choice is not a geography lesson. It is the ground where the strategy will spend force.

Choose the field where the win can become real, then let the other attractive fields wait outside the van.
breakdown.deepRead:
Keziah sits at a folding table after a parent night with three signup sheets: toddlers, teens, and adult beginners. Her art studio could serve all of them badly. When she chooses anxious middle-schoolers who need a quiet place after school, the room changes. The shelves, hours, prices, and teacher scripts start to fit one audience.

Where to play turns a broad dream into a bounded game. The boundary can be customer, channel, region, need, price, or occasion. The point is not to make the aim timid. The point is to pick ground where the way to win has a chance.

Picture Yuki at a farmers market stall with unsold jars of chili oil. Tourists praise the label and walk away. The ramen shop owner asks for a case and a wholesale sheet. The field may not be shoppers with tote bags. It may be small kitchens that need a finishing oil by Friday.

The trap is treating the old field as fate. It is often just habit with a map attached.

A dentist can say the practice serves families. That field sounds clear until the appointment book shows toddlers, teens with braces, anxious adults, and emergency crowns all competing for the same rooms. If the practice chooses working parents who need early pediatric cleanings, hours, reminders, toys, and insurance scripts start to line up. The field gives the team a design problem it can actually solve.
breakdown.fullRead:
Dalton stands inside a city bus depot at 5:52 a.m., watching route maps curl at the corners. His repair crew is good, but the contract bids cover school buses, airport shuttles, municipal buses, and private coaches across three counties. Each segment needs different parts, hours, and promises. The shop calls this growth. The mechanics call it Tuesday chaos.

Where to play is the choice that tells the rest of the strategy what game it is in. A company can choose high-end beauty buyers in airport retail, rural clinics needing simple diagnostics, parents of toddlers in dense neighborhoods, or contractors who need parts before sunrise. Each field changes what winning means and what capabilities matter.

Sohail learns it in a tenant-rights nonprofit. The group says it serves renters. That sounds focused until the phones show eviction defense, repair demands, lease questions, and senior housing confusion all piling into the same two staff members. Sohail chooses one field for the next grant cycle: eviction prevention for families with court dates inside fourteen days. The phone script changes. The volunteer training changes. The outreach partners change. The field is narrower, but the work finally has weight.

Maritza gets the warning on a college radio station. Alumni tell her the station has always served everyone on campus. That old map feels noble. It also leaves the schedule full of shows nobody can find twice. She chooses late-night commuters and lab students as the audience for live talk blocks. Some DJs complain. Then the message board fills after midnight.

Narrowing can be lazy if it only dodges hard work. A small field is not automatically a good field. It must be large enough to matter, reachable by the channels you can use, and matched to an advantage you can build.

When someone says the market is obvious, ask which slice of it you are refusing. The refusal is where the field becomes a choice.

Field choice also decides what you stop learning about. A team that chooses hospital kitchens for yogurt should learn ordering cycles, cooler space, food-service budgets, and chef frustrations. It should stop spending its best attention on weekend browsers who praise labels and buy nothing. Focus is not only where you sell. It is where you learn fastest.

The field has to be tested against reality. Is the segment large enough to matter? Can you reach it without spending more than the win is worth? Does your way to win fit the field, or are you choosing a customer who needs something else? A narrow field that fails these tests is not strategy. It is comfort.

A useful field often feels awkward at first because it disappoints someone. The cafe owner outside the field, the parent whose preferred hour changes, the donor who liked the old broad label. That discomfort is information. If the team can explain the field and the reason for refusing other fields, the strategy is becoming clear.

examples.title: Bruna folds the route map in the dairy cooler

planSpec.requiredBeat: choose one customer field for the van

examples.scenario: Bruna holds a wet route map against the dairy cooler door at 4:27 a.m., the paper curling from the cold. Six cafe pins dot the city, plus three hospital kitchens that pay on time. Her van can make one route before noon. The cafes love samples and haggle by text. The hospitals reorder every Thursday. She must choose whether the yogurt business is chasing charming counters or feeding kitchens that already know their volumes.
examples.whatToDo: Pick the field the van can serve reliably and profitably, then redesign sales around that field. Leave the other pins visible but outside the current route.
examples.whyItMatters: The route is the constraint that makes the field real. Bruna cannot build an advantage while pretending every pin deserves the same morning.

examples.title: Keziah stacks three signup sheets after parent night

planSpec.requiredBeat: too many age groups make the studio incoherent

examples.scenario: Keziah stacks three signup sheets at 8:39 p.m. after parent night in the church basement: toddlers, teens, and adults. The markers smell sharp, and the sample clay has dried around the edges. Her first month tried to serve all three. Toddlers needed cleanup time, teens needed quiet, adults wanted wine and critique. She circles the middle-school sheet and finally sees why every Saturday felt like three businesses in one room.
examples.whatToDo: Choose the age group and occasion where the studio can matter most, then rebuild hours, supplies, and teacher scripts around that field.
examples.whyItMatters: The studio was not failing from lack of interest. It was failing because one room was asked to host three different games. Field choice gives the offer a shape.

examples.title: Dalton hears the mechanic name four businesses
examples.scenario: Dalton stands by bay three at 5:52 a.m. while a mechanic wipes grease from his wrist. "School buses need us before homeroom," the mechanic says. "Airport shuttles need midnight parts. Coaches need upholstery. City buses need brake stock." Dalton has one bid packet in his hand for all four segments. The compressor kicks on. He faces a choice before the noon submission.
examples.whatToDo: Separate the segments by what they require, then bid only on the field the shop can support with real depth. Do not let one contract packet hide four businesses.
examples.whyItMatters: Different customers pull different capabilities from the shop. Dalton needs a field where the repair edge can show up every week, not a field that flatters the revenue line.

examples.title: Sohail sorts eviction calls by court date

planSpec.requiredBeat: renters is too broad; eviction court window is sharper

examples.scenario: Sohail predicted a renters hotline would focus the nonprofit. At 11:06 a.m. in the intake room, the call log says otherwise: mold, leases, rent hikes, senior housing, court summons. A volunteer points to a mother whose hearing is nine days away. The broad field is swallowing the urgent one. Sohail must decide whether next month's grant serves renters in general or families with court dates inside fourteen days.
examples.whatToDo: Choose the urgent field and design intake, partners, and scripts around it. Keep other renter problems in referral paths until the core work has enough force.
examples.whyItMatters: The chosen field changes what speed means. A family with a court date needs a different system than a caller with a broad lease question.

examples.title: Maritza turns the midnight callers into the audience

planSpec.requiredBeat: old broad campus field gives way to late-night audience

examples.scenario: At 12:17 a.m., Maritza watches the studio phone blink during a live call-in about lab shifts and bus rides. The old schedule tried to serve the whole campus and drew silence. She moves the strongest talk blocks after eleven, cuts three sleepy afternoon shows, and names the field: students awake when campus is closed. By October, the message board fills before the opening song ends.
examples.whatToDo: Let the audience that already responds define the field, then change the schedule enough that the choice can be felt.
examples.whyItMatters: The station did not need broader appeal. It needed a field with a real habit and a reason to listen at a specific hour.

examples.title: Yuki weighs tourist praise against ramen-shop orders

planSpec.requiredBeat: tourist retail loses to small kitchens

examples.scenario: Yuki lines up chili-oil jars at 9:44 a.m. under the farmers market tent. Tourists keep lifting the jars, praising the red label, and setting them back. Then the ramen shop owner from Halsey Street arrives with an empty crate and asks for twelve by Friday. Rain ticks on the canopy. Yuki can keep tuning the stall for weekend browsers or choose small kitchens as the field.
examples.whatToDo: Treat the reorder as evidence of a better field. Build pricing, packaging, and delivery for small kitchens before spending another month chasing compliments from browsers.
examples.whyItMatters: Praise is not the same as a field. The ramen owner shows a channel where the product solves a repeated problem and can build a position.

questions.prompt: A manager is staring at a planning slide with eight equal priorities and one budget line already cut. The team wants language that keeps every group happy before the Thursday review. Which action best applies the move?
choices: Force the slide to name the one choice that decides the rest.
Add a sentence saying all priorities remain important.
Delay the review until every leader has edited the slide.
questions.explanation: The right move makes the choice visible. A strategy that protects every claim cannot guide scarce money or attention.

questions.prompt: A teacher is picking projects for a six-week unit. Three options are useful, but only one fits the students she most wants to serve this term. What should she do first?
choices: Run all three as shorter projects.
Choose the project that fits the chosen students and let the others wait.
Ask students to vote without naming the learning target.
questions.explanation: The useful option is not always the strategic option. Fit to the chosen aim should lead the decision.

questions.prompt: A founder has a new offer, a thin cash balance, and two customer groups asking for different features by Friday. Which response best keeps the strategy coherent?
choices: Promise both groups a lighter version.
Build the feature requested by the louder group.
Pick the customer group tied to the win and say no to the other request.
questions.explanation: The move protects the chosen game. Saying yes to the wrong buyer can spend the same resources while weakening the path to win.

questions.prompt: A clinic team notices its dashboard is full of green marks, but patients in the chosen service line still wait too long. Which action fits the lesson?
choices: Change the measure so it tracks the wait that decides the chosen service line.
Celebrate the green dashboard to keep morale high.
Add a second dashboard for every department.
questions.explanation: Measures should support the actual choice. A green report that misses the chosen result trains the team to drift politely.

questions.prompt: A parent is helping a teenager plan summer activities. The list has sports, coding, travel, work, and test prep, all marked urgent. What is the best next move?
choices: Rank the activities by how impressive they sound.
Name the one summer outcome that should lead the schedule.
Keep all activities and shorten sleep for two weeks.
questions.explanation: A clear leading aim makes the rest easier to sort. Without it, every good option claims the same space.

questions.prompt: A nonprofit board wants to serve seniors, new immigrants, artists, and local schools with one small grant. Which plan best follows the move?
choices: Split the grant into four equal mini-programs.
Use the grant on the group with the loudest advocate.
Choose one audience and design the program to win trust there first.
questions.explanation: Small resources need a field. Equal spread can feel fair while making the work too weak for anyone.

questions.prompt: A restaurant owner is choosing between faster lunch service, a deeper dinner menu, and catering. The kitchen can support only one new habit this month. What should she do?
choices: Choose the habit that reinforces the desired position with customers.
Try all three and review after staff burn out.
Let each shift choose its own priority.
questions.explanation: The best action reinforces the same edge. A kitchen cannot learn three different games at once.

questions.prompt: A student group has survey data, interview notes, and pricing guesses, but nobody has written the actual options on the wall. Which move should come next?
choices: Collect more survey answers before speaking.
Write two or three real options and use the evidence to test them.
Pick the safest option because it has fewer objections.
questions.explanation: Evidence needs options to judge. More facts do not help until the group names the paths it might take.

questions.prompt: A designer wants confidence before narrowing a product concept. She can test one assumption with five users tomorrow. Which plan best fits the move?
choices: Wait until the full prototype is polished.
Ask friends which concept sounds more exciting.
Test the assumption that would kill the concept if it fails.
questions.explanation: The strongest test puts pressure on the condition that carries the decision. It improves the odds faster than broad reassurance.

reviewCards.front: You see a plan with many good options and no lead choice. What question should you ask first?
reviewCards.back: Ask which result or customer is allowed to decide the next tradeoff. The answer should make at least one attractive option fall behind.

reviewCards.front: A team says every priority matters equally. How do you test whether where to play is real?
reviewCards.back: Look for a resource shift, a narrower field, or a changed routine. If nothing changes after the words are approved, the choice is still soft.

reviewCards.front: A colleague objects that narrowing the plan feels risky. What answer keeps the work practical?
reviewCards.back: Say that narrowing is not about being small. It is about putting force behind the field where the team has the best chance to win.

reviewCards.front: You have one week before a review and too many claims in the plan. What should be on your scratch pad?
reviewCards.back: Write the chosen win, field, edge, needed capabilities, and management checks. Then mark any claim that does not support that chain.

implementationPlan.coreSkill: The skill is field selection. You learn to choose the customer, channel, place, occasion, or price tier where advantage can actually grow.

ifThenPlans.plan: If a meeting starts with a list of equal priorities, then ask which one choice should receive money, people, or calendar time first.
If you add a new routine, then name the one health result it serves and remove one routine that does not help that result this month.
If your weekend plan has more than three serious goals, then choose the one goal that would make Sunday night feel won and schedule it first.
If a shared plan is getting broad and polite, then ask what both of you are willing to stop doing so the chosen aim has room.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: Before the next planning conversation, write the customer, channel, place, and occasion you are choosing for one active plan. Circle the one answer that should force a real tradeoff, then bring only that circled choice to the room.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: For seven days, keep a one-page choice log. Each time a plan grows wider, write the choice, the option you refused, and what changed because you refused it.
